value: 15 % CH4 in N2 ignites in 30 % O2 but extinguishes soon after
quote: For 15% CH4 / 85% N2, flames are ignited, but extinguish soon after.

value: 250 C: with helium diluent the burner reached its temperature limit and the automated protocol ended many tests before extinction
quote: the automated protocol ended the tests as the burner temperature routinely reached 250°C.

value: 1130 K: every ISS flame (normal and inverse ethylene) went out at this peak temperature
quote: All the ISS flames observed by this project extinguish at a critical extinction temperature of 1130 K

value: 0.2 g/m2-s fuel flux (normal flames), 0.68 g/m2-s oxygen flux (inverse flames) at extinction
quote: and at a fuel mass flux of 0.2 g/m2-s for normal flames, and at an oxygen mass flux of 0.68 g/m2-s for inverse flames

value: radiative extinction: a flame fed at constant flow grows until radiation loss matches heat release
quote: Radiative extinction is observed when, at constant reactant flow rate, the flame expands until radiation heat loss approaches the chemical heat release.

value: flames oscillate (partial extinction and reforming) before going out completely
quote: Before a flame experiences complete extinction, it may enter an oscillatory mode in which part of the flame partially extinguishes and then reforms.

value: 870 s: longest steady-state flame observed on the ISS; small flames can burn steadily
quote: flames that exhibit steady-state behavior are observed aboard the ISS for up to 870 s, even with the constraint of a finite boundary.

value: small quasi-steady flames last until the burner overheats, not until they self-extinguish
quote: Sufficiently small flames with low radiation losses exhibit quasi-steady behavior, but burner heating is significant, and the experimental duration is dictated by the temperature limit of the porous sphere.

value: pressure is a critical variable for predicting flame extinction
quote: Our recent analysis suggests that pressure is a critical variable when predicting flame extinction

value: about 2 of 16 tests per day failed to ignite or did not sustain ignition
quote: An average of 16 tests were conducted per Flame Design test day, where ignition was typically unsuccessful (e.g., un-sustained) in a couple of tests.

value: without buoyancy, radiative extinction dominates and matters for spacecraft fire safety
quote: In microgravity combustion, where buoyancy is not present to accelerate the flow field and strain the flame, radiative extinction is of fundamental importance, and has implications for spacecraft fire safety.

value: 2 bar, 39% O2: only condition (normal n-butane flames) giving spherical cool diffusion flames
quote: However, these CDFs were not readily produced and were only obtained for normal n-butane flames at 2 bar with an ambient oxygen mole fraction of 0.39.

value: 2.6: hot flames that spawned cool flames were 2.6 times as large
quote: The hot flames that spawned the CDFs were 2.6 times as large.

value: a cool flame can keep burning after the hot flame self-extinguishes
quote: non-premixed cool flames can be directly ignited by limiting the ignition energy or can occur after the self-extinguishment of (normal) hot flames.

value: cool flames went unnoticed during operations; found in data review days later
quote: evidence of cool flames was first discovered in review of the data a few days after the testing.

value: hot flames reignited repeatedly from the invisible low-temperature combustion
quote: two of the tests exhibited repeated hot flame quenching and reignition, which resulting from intervening low-temperature combustion.

value: a platinum (type B) thermocouple catalysed the reignition of hot flames
quote: The exposed type-B thermocouple includes platinum, a catalyst for the oxidation of hydrocarbons.

value: 30 s of microgravity needed for quasi-steady spherical flames (drop towers give 5 s)
quote: approximately 30 s of jitter-free (less than 10-5 g) microgravity is needed to approach quasi-steady state for these flames.

value: 6 hot-flame reignitions (via cool flames) in one n-butane test at 2 bar, 40% O2, until the fuel was cut
quote: hot flame extinguished & reignited repeatedly until we simply stopped the fuel flow

value: 700 to 900 K: droplet cool flames burn without a visible flame (hot flames above 1200 K)
quote: quasi-steady stable flames can be established surrounding a droplet in microgravity under certain conditions, without a visible flame at temperatures in the range of 700 to 900 K, unlike the hot flames where the flame temperature is higher than 1200 K

value: warm flames after radiative extinction at higher pressure are not visible to the color camera
quote: Warm flames were observed typically at higher pressures following radiative extinction and the flame is not visible in the color camera.

value: cool flame ends at a finite droplet size; unburned fuel vaporizes and a vapor cloud of partially oxidized fuel forms
quote: abruptly ends at a finite droplet diameter, leaving the unburned droplet to vaporize in the hot atmosphere. A vapor cloud was also found to form around the droplet as the partially oxidized fuel condensed immediately following cool-flame extinction.

value: cool flames need long residence times and are not seen with droplet flames in normal gravity
quote: the cool flames need much longer residence times and cannot be observed under normal gravity conditions with droplet flames.

value: 2 atm: above it, hot flame and cool flame alternate through repeated reignitions until the droplet is consumed
quote: as the ambient pressure is increased above 2 atm, multiple reignition cycles were observed, where first the hot flame extinguishes due to radiative heat loss followed by cool flame, and then reignition to a hot-flame followed by a cool flame, with this cycle repeating several times until the fuel droplet is completely consumed.

value: 4 mm initial droplets were used so that radiative extinction and the following cool flame occur
quote: The initial droplet size was kept around 4 mm so that radiative extinction and the subsequent cool flame combustion can be observed.

value: adding iso-dodecane to n-dodecane reduces cool flame formation
quote: The addition of iso-dodecanol reduces the tendency to form cool flames in n-dodecanol.

value: more helium dilution makes the cool flame go out earlier, at a larger droplet diameter
quote: Increase helium dilution leads to earlier cool flame extinction giving a larger extinction diameter.

value: 40 micron support fiber has little effect on the cool flame extinction diameter
quote: It is interesting to note that the 40 micron fiber shows relatively little effect on the extinction diameter.

value: at higher pressure residual soot stays around the droplet after hot flame extinction; soot shell becomes diffuse
quote: when the pressure increases, residual soot is seen surrounding the droplet even after the hot flame extinction.

value: at low pressure the cool flame forms no soot; hot flame soot is carried away from the droplet
quote: At low pressures, due to the low flame temperature of the cool flame, soot is not formed. The soot that is formed during the hot flame combustion is simply convected away from the droplet surface.

value: all 5 materials: sub-micron smoke readily seen by an ionization detector
quote: all samples produced significant numbers of sub-micron particulate that are readily detected using an ionization smoke detector

value: aged silicone rubber smoke grows to sizes better seen by light scattering
quote: the aging results suggest that some materials such as silicone rubber can produce smoke that can reach sizes better detected by light scattering techniques

value: Kapton and Teflon smoke too small for reliable light-scattering detection
quote: The comparatively much smaller diameters for the Kapton and Teflon will make detection of this smoke challenging for light scattering devices

value: lampwick and silicone smoke give very large light-scattering signals
quote: the large sizes seen with the lamp wick and silicone would generate very large signals on a light scattering system

value: measure 2 or more moments of the size distribution to detect all smokes and reject dust
quote: These results suggest that detection methods that can measure more than one moment of the size distribution may show more successful detection and false alarm rejection than single moment detectors.

value: 2-moment MPASS prototype tells dense smoke from sparse large dust
quote: The MPASS therefore has the ability to discern the difference between a strong signal from a high smoke concentration and a strong signal from a lower concentration of very large dust particles, a feature which can minimize false smoke detector alarms.

value: 2 to 3x larger particles with no air flow than at 8 cm/s

value: 30 to 40 % larger diameter of average mass at zero flow, all materials
quote: It is found for all of the materials the diameter of average mass is 30 % to 40 % larger for the zero-flow tests compared to the flow tests.

value: zero-flow smoke growth is specific to low gravity (no buoyant mixing)
